entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3577"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 23</title> <div sID="gen5094" type="x-p"/> <reference osisRef="2Kgs.23.1-2Kgs.23.3">2Ki 23:1-3</reference>. Josiah Causes the Law to Be Read.<div eID="gen5094" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5095" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3577"/><hi type="bold">1-3. the king sent, and they gathered unto him all the elders--</hi>This pious and patriotic king, not content with the promise of his own security, felt, after Huldah's response, an increased desire to avert the threatened calamities from his kingdom and people. Knowing the richness of the divine clemency and grace to the penitent, he convened the elders of the people, and placing himself at their head, accompanied by the collective body of the inhabitants, went in solemn procession to the temple, where he ordered the book of the law to be read to the assembled audience, and covenanted, with the unanimous concurrence of his subjects, to adhere steadfastly to all the commandments of the Lord. It was an occasion of solemn interest, closely connected with a great national crisis, and the beautiful example of piety in the highest quarter would exert a salutary influence over all classes of the people in animating their devotions and encouraging their return to the faith of their fathers. <div eID="gen5095" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3580"/><div sID="gen5099" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3580"/><hi type="bold">4. the king commanded Hilkiah, &c.--</hi>that is, the high priest and other priests, for there was not a variety of official gradations in the temple.<div eID="gen5099" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5100" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">all the vessels, &c.--</hi>the whole apparatus of idol-worship.<div eID="gen5100" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5101" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">burned them without Jerusalem--</hi>The law required them to be consigned to the flames (<reference osisRef="Deut.7.25">De 7:25</reference>).<div eID="gen5101" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5102" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">in the fields of Kidron--</hi>most probably that part of the valley of Kidron, where lies Jerusalem and the Mount of Olives. It is a level, spacious basin, abounding at present with plantations [Robinson]. The brook winds along the east and south of the city, the channel of which is throughout a large portion of the year almost or wholly dry, except after heavy rains, when it suddenly swells and overflows. There were emptied all the impurities of the temple (<reference osisRef="2Chr.29.15">2Ch 29:15</reference>, <reference osisRef="2Chr.29.16">16</reference>) and the city. His reforming predecessors had ordered the mutilated relics of idolatry to be thrown into that receptacle of filth (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.15.13">1Ki 15:13</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.15.16">2Ch 15:16</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Chr.30.14">30:14</reference>); but Josiah, while he imitated their piety, far outstripped them in zeal; for he caused the ashes of the burnt wood and the fragments of the broken metal to be collected and conveyed to Beth-el, in order thenceforth to associate ideas of horror and aversion with that place, as odious for the worst pollutions. <div eID="gen5102" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3582"/><div sID="gen5106" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3582"/><hi type="bold">6. brought out the grove--</hi>that is, Asherah, the mystic tree, placed by Manasseh in the temple [2Ki 21:5; 2Ch 33:5], removed by him after his conversion [2Ch 33:15], but replaced in the sanctuary by his wicked son Amon [2Ki 21:20, 21]. Josiah had it taken to Kidron, burnt the wood, ground the metal about it to powder, and strewed the ashes "on the graves of the children of the people." The poor were buried in a common on part of the valley of Kidron. But reference is here made to the graves "of those that had sacrificed" (<reference osisRef="2Chr.34.4">2Ch 34:4</reference>). <div eID="gen5106" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3583"/><div sID="gen5107" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3583"/><hi type="bold">7. brake down the houses of the sodomites--</hi>not solid houses, but tents, called elsewhere [2Ki 17:30] Succoth-benoth, "the booths of the young women," who were devoted to the service of Asherah, for which they made embroidered hangings, and in which they gave themselves to unbridled revelry and lust. entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3584"/><div sID="gen5108" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3584"/><hi type="bold">8-9. he brought all the priests out of the cities of Judah, and defiled the high places, &c.--</hi>Many of the Levitical order, finding in the reigns of Manasseh and Amon the temple-worship abolished and the tithes and other offerings alienated, had been betrayed into the folly of officiating on high places, and presenting such sacrifices as were brought to them. These irregularities, even though the object of that worship was the true God, were prohibited in the law (<reference osisRef="Deut.12.11">De 12:11</reference>). Those who had been guilty of this sin, Josiah brought to Jerusalem. Regarding them as defiled, he debarred them from the service of the temple, but gave them an allowance out of the temple revenues, like the lame and disabled members of the priesthood (<reference osisRef="Lev.21.21">Le 21:21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Lev.21.22">22</reference>).<div eID="gen5108" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5109" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">from Geba to to Beer-sheba--</hi>the most northern and the most southern places in Judah--meaning all parts of the kingdom.<div eID="gen5109" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5110" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the high places ... which were in the entering in of the gate of Joshua--</hi>The governor's house and gate were on the left of the city gate, and close by the entrance of that civic mansion house were public altars, dedicated, it might be, to the true God, but contrary to His own ordinance of worship (<reference osisRef="Isa.57.8">Is 57:8</reference>). <div eID="gen5110" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3586"/><div sID="gen5112" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3586"/><hi type="bold">11. took away the horses that the kings of Judah had given to the sun--</hi>Among the people who anciently worshipped the sun, horses were usually dedicated to that divinity, from the supposed idea that the sun himself was drawn in a chariot by horses. In some cases these horses were sacrificed; but more commonly they were employed either in the sacred processions to carry the images of the sun, or for the worshippers to ride in every morning to welcome his rise. It seems that the idolatrous kings, Ahaz, Manasseh, and Amon, or their great officers, proceeded on these horses early on each day from the east gate of the temple to salute and worship the sun at his appearing above the horizon. <div eID="gen5112" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3588"/><div sID="gen5114" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3588"/><hi type="bold">13-14. the high places ... which Solomon ... had builded--</hi>(See on <reference osisRef="1Kgs.11.5">1Ki 11:5</reference>).<div eID="gen5114" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen5115" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the right hand of the mount of corruption--</hi>The Mount of Olives is a hilly range on the east of Jerusalem. This range has three summits, of which the central one is the Mount of Corruption, so called from the idol temples built there, and of course the hill on the right hand denotes the southernmost peak. Josiah is said not to have destroyed, but only defiled, "the high places on the hill of corruption." It is most probable that Hezekiah had long before demolished the idolatrous temples erected there by Solomon but, as the superstitious people continued to regard the spot as consecrated ground, Josiah defiled it. <div eID="gen5115" type="x-p"/>

entries.content_osis: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv3594"/><div sID="gen5122" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv3594"/><hi type="bold">26. Notwithstanding, the Lord turned not from the fierceness of his wrath,--</hi>&c. The national reformation which Josiah carried on was acquiesced in by the people from submission to the royal will; but they entertained a secret and strong hankering after the suppressed idolatries. Though outwardly purified, their hearts were not right towards God, as appears from many passages of the prophetic writings; their thorough reform was hopeless; and God, who saw no sign of genuine repentance, allowed His decree (<reference osisRef="2Kgs.21.12-2Kgs.21.15">2Ki 21:12-15</reference>) for the subversion of the kingdom to take fatal effect. <div eID="gen5122" type="x-p"/>
